verse.text: In many parts and in many ways God spoke long ago to our ancestors by the prophets,
but in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom he also made the universe.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “the ages”. The word is normally a time-word, but as the object of God’s making it denotes the whole created order through all its eras. Standard lexicons recognize this sense here and at Hebrews 11:3, and many modern versions also have “universe” or “world”.

verse.text: He is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of his being, and he sustains all things by his powerful word. Having made purification for sins through himself, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verse.note: The Greek word can mean light shining out from a source (“radiance”) or light thrown back from a surface (“reflection”). Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take it in the active sense of radiance, but “reflection” is possible and some versions use it.

The word was used for the impression stamped by a die or seal, as on a coin, which reproduces the original exactly. The Son is said to correspond to God’s actual being as a stamped impression corresponds to its die.

The Greek is literally “the word of power”, a Semitic-style construction in which the second noun describes the first. English expresses this more naturally with an adjective. The meaning is not in dispute.

Manuscripts differ here. Some have only “his” attached to “word of power”. Others have “through himself” with the purification, in addition to “his” or in place of it. The edition translated here reads “through himself”, and the sense of “his powerful word” is the same either way.

verse.text: having become as far superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son; today I have become your Father”? Or again, “I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to me”?

note.term: today I have become your Father

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for a father producing a child. “Begotten” is exact but no longer current English, so the clause is recast. Most formal translations still have “begotten”. The line quotes Psalm 2:7, where it is spoken to Israel’s king at his enthronement. The second quotation is from 2 Samuel 7:14.

verse.text: And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”
verse.note: “Again” may simply introduce a further quotation, as in verse 5, or it may modify the verb: “when he again brings the firstborn into the world”. On the second reading the reference would be to Christ’s return or his exaltation, not his first coming. The Greek word order slightly favors the second reading, but the author’s habit of using “again” to link quotations favors the first, and interpreters are divided.

note.term: Let all God’s angels worship him.

verse.note: This line does not appear in the standard Hebrew text of the Old Testament. It comes from the Greek version of Deuteronomy 32:43, and a similar line stands in Psalm 97:7. The author regularly quotes Scripture in its Greek form.

verse.text: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.”
verse.note: The same Greek word means both “wind” and “spirit”. In Psalm 104:4, quoted here, the pairing with “flame of fire” points to winds, and most modern versions translate it so. The author then plays on the other sense in verse 14, where the angels are “ministering spirits”.

verse.text: But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, and the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.
verse.note: The Greek can also be read “God is your throne” or “Your throne is God”. Most translators and commentators take “God” as an address to the Son, which fits the author’s argument and the address “Lord” in verse 10. The alternative is grammatically possible, and a minority defends it. The quotation is Psalm 45:6–7.

A few early and important manuscripts read “his kingdom”. That reading would fit better with “God is your throne” in the first line. Most manuscripts read “your”, as does the Greek text translated here.

text.q: You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

verse.text: And, “In the beginning, Lord, you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.

text.q: They will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment,
and like a cloak you will roll them up, and like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will never end.”

verse.text: And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”?
Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?
Therefore we must pay all the more attention to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.
For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and act of disobedience received a just penalty,
how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? It was first spoken through the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard him,
while God added his testimony by signs and wonders and various deeds of power, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power”, used in the plural for acts that display it. “Deeds of power” keeps that connection visible and keeps the word distinct from “signs” and “wonders” beside it. “Miracles” is the more common rendering and is equally accurate; the meaning is not in dispute.

verse.text: For it was not to angels that he subjected the world to come, about which we are speaking.
But someone has testified somewhere, saying, “What is a human being that you remember him, or a son of man that you care for him?
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 8:4–6 in its Greek form, where “a son of man” is a Semitic way of saying “a human being” and stands parallel to the first line. It is left lowercase because the psalm speaks of humankind, though the author goes on to find its fulfillment in Jesus (verse 9). Whether “him” in verse 8 refers to humanity in general or already to Jesus is disputed, and the translation leaves both readings open.

text.q: You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor;

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “a little” in degree or “for a little while” in time. The Hebrew psalm means the former, but the author’s argument in verse 9, where the lowering of Jesus is followed by his crowning, favors the temporal sense. Translations are divided.

verse.text: you subjected all things under his feet.” For in subjecting all things, he left nothing unsubjected to him. As it is, we do not yet see all things subjected to him.
But we do see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that apart from God he might taste death for everyone.
verse.note: The SBLGNT reads “apart from God” here. The great majority of manuscripts read “by the grace of God”, and nearly all English translations follow them. “Apart from God” survives in only a few manuscripts but was known to early Christian writers, Origen among them, and some scholars judge it the more difficult and therefore earlier reading. If original, it may mean that Jesus died abandoned by God, or that he died for everyone with God alone excepted.

verse.text: For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons and daughters to glory, should perfect the pioneer of their salvation through sufferings.
verse.note: The Greek has simply “sons”, which echoes the title “Son” given to Jesus in chapter one. The plural was regularly used for children of both sexes, and the author plainly has the whole community in view. “Sons and daughters” makes that clear at the cost of the verbal echo.

The verb means to bring someone to an intended goal or completed state, not to remove a moral flaw. Scholars agree on that much, but they differ on whether Hebrews also intends an overtone of priestly consecration, a sense the word has in the Greek Old Testament, or is thinking of Jesus being fully fitted for his role as savior and high priest.

verse.text: For the one who makes holy and those who are made holy are all from one. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters,
verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the word “holy” and means to bring someone into the sphere of what belongs to God. “Sanctify” is the traditional rendering and is accurate, but it hides the link with “holy” and now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement. Several modern translations also use “make holy” here.

The Greek says only “from one”, without saying one what. Most interpreters take it as one Father, that is, God; others take it as one human ancestor, such as Adam or Abraham, or as one common origin or family. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

The Greek plural was the ordinary way to refer to siblings of both sexes, and by extension to all members of a community. “Brothers” alone now sounds exclusively male in English, so the fuller phrase is used here and in verses 12 and 17. Many translations keep “brothers”.

verse.text: saying, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers and sisters; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise.”
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 22:22, where the Greek word denotes Israel gathered for worship. It is the same word the New Testament uses for the Christian community, usually translated “church”. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one word; “church” is the near-universal rendering elsewhere and is not wrong.

verse.text: And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Here am I, and the children God has given me.”

Since, then, the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise took part in the same things, so that through death he might render powerless the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,
verse.note: The verb means to put something out of operation or strip it of force; it is not the ordinary Greek word for destroying. Many translations have “destroy” here, but the devil is not said to cease to exist, only to lose his hold. The rendering also echoes “the power of death” that follows, though the Greek uses two unrelated words.

verse.text: and set free those who all their lives were held in slavery by the fear of death.
For surely it is not angels that he takes hold of; rather, he takes hold of the offspring of Abraham.

note.traditional: took on him the nature of (KJV); helps (most modern versions)

verse.note: The verb means to take hold of or grasp someone. Most modern translations understand this as taking hold in order to help, and render it “helps”. An older interpretation took it as taking on a nature, that is, becoming human rather than angelic. The literal rendering is kept because the same verb is used in 8:9 of God taking Israel by the hand.

verse.text: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers and sisters in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in matters relating to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.
verse.note: Older translations have “make propitiation” or “make reconciliation” for the sins of the people. Scholars have long debated whether this word family means propitiation (turning away divine wrath) or expiation (removing sin). Here the direct object is “sins”, and “make atonement” reflects the priestly language of the Greek Old Testament without deciding the wider debate.

verse.text: For because he himself has suffered when tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel’s testing in the wilderness, a background Hebrews draws on in the next chapters. Most translations have “tempted” here, and the lexicons recognize both senses. “Tested” was chosen because the context is suffering, and “tempt” in modern English has narrowed to enticement to sin.

verse.text: Therefore, holy brothers and sisters, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as fellow members of a family or community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Several modern translations make the same choice, while others keep “brothers.”

verse.text: who was faithful to the one who appointed him, just as Moses also was in his house.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for “make,” so the phrase can be read “the one who made him.” Most translators and commentators take it here in the sense “appoint to an office,” a use found in the Greek Old Testament, since the context concerns Jesus’ role as apostle and high priest. The other reading was debated in antiquity and remains grammatically possible.

The wording echoes Numbers 12:7, where God says of Moses, “he is faithful in all my house.” “His house” is therefore God’s house, meaning God’s household or people and not a building. The same word carries both senses, “house” and “household,” throughout verses 2–6.

verse.text: For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, by as much as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.
For every house is built by someone, but the one who built all things is God.
Now Moses was faithful in all his house as a servant, to bear witness to the things that would be spoken later,
but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house. And we are that house, if we hold fast our confidence and the hope in which we boast.

note.term: the hope in which we boast
note.traditional: the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “firm to the end” after “hope,” and older English versions include it. Some early witnesses lack the words, and they are widely thought to have been copied in from verse 14, where the same phrase appears. The edition translated here omits them.

verse.text: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear his voice,

text.q: do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness,

verse.note: The quotation in verses 7–11 is Psalm 95:7–11 in its Greek form. The Hebrew psalm names two places, Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7), but the Greek version translates the names as common nouns: “rebellion” (or “embittering”) and “testing.” Readers of the Greek heard a description of what Israel did, not place names.

Older versions have “the day of temptation” here and “tempted me” in verse 9. The Greek noun and its related verb mean putting someone to the proof, and here it is Israel that tries God’s patience, which “temptation” in its modern sense of enticement to sin does not convey. Most modern translations also use “testing” in this passage.

text.q: where your ancestors put me to the test and tried me, and saw my works
for forty years. Therefore I was provoked with this generation and said, ‘They always go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways.’

verse.note: In the psalm, “forty years” goes with what follows: God was provoked with that generation for forty years. As quoted here, with “therefore” added after it, the phrase goes with what precedes: the ancestors saw God’s works for forty years. In verse 17 the author also connects the forty years with God’s being provoked, so he appears to hold both together.

text.q: As I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest.’”

note.term: They shall never enter my rest
note.traditional: They shall not enter into my rest

verse.note: The Greek reads literally “if they shall enter my rest,” reproducing a Hebrew oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken (“may such-and-such happen to me if…”). The effect is an emphatic denial. The oath itself is recounted in Numbers 14:20–35, after Israel refused to enter the land.

verse.text: See to it, brothers and sisters, that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
Instead, encourage one another every day, as long as it is called “Today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold fast our original resolve, firm to the end.
verse.note: The Greek noun can mean one who shares in something or a partner alongside someone. The phrase can therefore mean “we share in Christ” or “we have become Christ’s partners.” The rendering here matches verse 1, where the same word is used of sharing in a heavenly calling, but both readings have scholarly support.

Most English versions render “our original confidence” or “conviction.” In the usage of the period, however, the word normally names something objective, such as a firm stand or a course one has committed to, and lexicographers have questioned whether the sense of an inner feeling of confidence is securely attested. “Resolve” reflects the firm-stand sense and suits the call to hold fast to the end. Scholarship is divided and “confidence” remains defensible.

verse.text: As it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
For who were those who heard and rebelled? Was it not all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses?

note.term: For who were those who heard and rebelled?
note.traditional: For some, when they had heard, did provoke: howbeit not all that came out of Egypt by Moses

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts had no accents, and the first word can be read either as “who?” or as “some.” Older versions took it as a statement: “some rebelled, but not all.” Nearly all modern editors and translators read a question, which matches the two parallel questions in verses 17 and 18.

verse.text: And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses fell in the wilderness?
And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, if not to those who disobeyed?
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
So let us be afraid that, while the promise of entering his rest still remains, any one of you might be found to have fallen short of it.
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean “seem,” “think,” or “be judged.” The rendering takes it in the last sense, of a verdict that someone has missed the promise. Others translate “should seem to have fallen short,” or, less often, “should think he has come too late for it.”

verse.text: For we too have had good news announced to us, just as they did; but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.

note.term: had good news announced to us
note.traditional: had the gospel preached to us

verse.note: The verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, and here it is applied equally to the wilderness generation and to the readers. “Gospel” would suggest a specifically Christian message that Israel in the desert did not hear in that form. Many modern translations already use “good news” here.

note.term: because they were not united by faith with those who listened
note.traditional: not being mixed with faith in them that heard it

verse.note: The manuscripts differ by one ending. The reading followed here makes the people “not united” with those who listened, probably Joshua and Caleb or believers generally. The other reading makes the message “not combined with faith in those who heard it,” and several major translations follow it. The first has the stronger early manuscript support, though the second gives a smoother sense, and the choice is disputed.

verse.text: For we who have believed do enter that rest, just as he has said: “As I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest,’” although his works had been finished since the foundation of the world.

note.term: They shall never enter my rest

verse.note: The Greek literally reads “If they shall enter my rest,” copying a Hebrew oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken. The form amounts to an emphatic denial. The quotation is Psalm 95:11 (94:11 in the Greek Old Testament), which looks back to the wilderness generation barred from Canaan.

verse.text: For somewhere he has spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,”
and again in this passage: “They shall never enter my rest.”
Since, then, it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly had the good news announced to them did not enter because of disobedience,
he again fixes a certain day—“Today”—saying through David so long afterward, as has been said before, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day.
verse.note: In Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are identical (Iēsous). The context, the entry into Canaan, shows that Joshua son of Nun is meant, but a first-century hearer would have caught the echo of Jesus’ name. The older English rendering “Jesus” here is misleading.

verse.text: So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God;
verse.note: The author switches here from the word for “rest” used throughout the passage to a rare noun that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. In later Greek writers it means Sabbath observance. Some therefore prefer “Sabbath celebration” or “Sabbath keeping,” but “Sabbath rest” is the usual rendering and ties the word to God’s seventh-day rest in verse 4.

verse.text: for whoever has entered God’s rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his own.
Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by following the same example of disobedience.

For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
No creature is hidden from his sight, but everything is naked and laid bare to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.
verse.note: The verb is formed from the word for “neck” and occurs only here in the New Testament. Elsewhere it is used of a wrestler seizing an opponent by the neck. The image intended here is uncertain, with suggestions including a wrestler’s hold and a sacrificial victim’s throat bent back and exposed. The general sense of being fully exposed is agreed.

note.term: to whom we must give account
note.traditional: with whom we have to do

verse.note: The Greek is literally “to whom, for us, the word,” using the same noun, logos, that opens verse 12 (“the word of God”). It can mean “to whom we must render account” or, as a common idiom, “with whom we have to do.” The first fits the judicial imagery of the passage, and either way the author is playing on the two senses of the noun.

verse.text: Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession.
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every way just as we are, yet without sin.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the standard word for the testing of Israel in the wilderness, the story the author has just been expounding. Modern English “tempt” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Most translations keep “tempted” here, partly because of the following “yet without sin,” and lexicons recognize both senses, so the choice is disputed.

verse.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us at the right time.
verse.note: The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind and came to mean the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Boldness” can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point. Several modern versions also have “confidence” here, and the difference is one of English nuance, not a dispute about meaning.

verse.text: For every high priest taken from among people is appointed on behalf of people in matters relating to God, to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and straying, since he himself is also clothed with weakness,
verse.note: The Law of Moses provided sacrifices for sins committed unknowingly or by going astray, and distinguished these from deliberate, defiant sin. The phrase points to that category of sinner, the kind a high priest's offerings were meant to cover.

verse.text: and because of it he is obliged to make offerings for sins, as for the people, so also for himself.
And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
So also Christ did not glorify himself in becoming high priest; rather, it was the one who said to him, “You are my Son; today I have fathered you,”
verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 2:7, where God addresses the king at his enthronement. “Begotten” is the traditional word and remains in many translations, but it is no longer current English; “fathered” gives the same meaning. Some modern versions have “today I have become your Father.”

verse.text: just as he also says in another place, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”

note.term: according to the order of Melchizedek

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:4. Melchizedek is the priest-king of Genesis 14, who stands outside the line of Aaron. The Greek word rendered “order” means rank, arrangement or kind; it does not imply a succession of priests, and many scholars take the sense here to be “of the same kind as Melchizedek.”

verse.text: In the days of his flesh, Christ offered prayers and pleas, with a loud cry and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.

note.traditional: in that he feared / because of his reverent submission

verse.note: The Greek word can mean reverent awe toward God or, less often, anxious fear. Most scholars and translations take it as here: his prayer was heard because of his reverence. A minority read “he was heard and set free from his fear.”

verse.text: Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from what he suffered,

note.term: learned obedience from what he suffered

verse.note: The Greek words for “learned” and “suffered” (emathen, epathen) rhyme, and pairing them was a familiar saying in Greek literature: one learns by suffering. The author applies the commonplace to the Son.

verse.text: and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,
verse.note: The verb means to bring someone to an intended goal or finished state, not to remove moral faults. Here it describes Christ being fully fitted for his role as high priest through what he suffered; scholars differ on how far it also echoes the Greek Old Testament's language for consecrating priests. “The mature” in verse 14 belongs to the same word family.

verse.text: addressed by God as high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

note.traditional: designated by God / called of God

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means to address or greet someone by a name or title. Most translations have “designated” or “called,” which is also defensible. “Addressed” keeps the link to the psalm just quoted, in which God speaks to him directly: “You are a priest forever.”

verse.text: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become sluggish in hearing.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can be masculine (“about him,” meaning Melchizedek or Christ) or neuter (“about this,” meaning the subject of this high priesthood). Translations are divided, and the difference in meaning is slight.

verse.text: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the first elements of God’s oracles. You have come to need milk, not solid food.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, and the Greek word here can be read as “someone” or as “what.” With the second reading the sense is “you need to be taught what the first elements of God's oracles are.” The edition translated here, with most modern versions, reads “someone.”

verse.text: For everyone who lives on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for that person is an infant.
verse.note: The phrase is open to several readings: teaching about righteousness, the ability to reason about what is right (compare “distinguish good from evil” in verse 14), or, continuing the picture of the infant, correct speech. The literal form is kept so as not to close off the options. Greek has one word family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice).

verse.text: But solid food is for the mature, for those who because of their mature condition have their faculties trained to distinguish good from evil.

note.traditional: by reason of use / by constant practice

verse.note: Most translations render this “by practice” or “by constant use.” In Greek of the period, however, the word regularly means a state or condition of body or mind, often the settled condition that results from training, and not the activity of practicing. Lexicographers have argued that “practice” is a long-standing mistake here, and the standard lexicon now gives “mature state.”

verse.text: So then, let us leave behind the basic message about Christ and be carried on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of turning back from dead works and of faith in God,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek, echoing the prophets’ call to return to God, describes a change of direction in mind and conduct. Here it is a turning away “from dead works,” paired with faith directed toward God.

Older versions have “perfection”; most modern translations have “maturity,” which fits the contrast just drawn between infants on milk and adults on solid food (5:13–14). The word also belongs to a theme of “completeness” or “perfection” that runs through Hebrews, and some interpreters think that fuller sense is in view here as well.

verse.text: instruction about washings and the laying on of hands, about the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.
verse.note: A few early manuscripts read “instruction” in a form that sets it alongside “foundation,” so that the instruction about washings, laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment is itself the foundation; this is the reading translated. Most manuscripts read “of instruction,” making it one more item in the list of what the foundation consists of. The difference in meaning is slight.

Many translations have “baptisms.” The Greek word here is plural and is not the usual New Testament noun for Christian baptism; elsewhere it is used of Jewish ritual washings (Hebrews 9:10; Mark 7:4). The instruction probably concerned how Christian baptism differed from other purification rites, though the exact reference is uncertain.

verse.text: And this we will do, if indeed God permits.
For it is impossible, when people have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and become sharers in the Holy Spirit,
and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age,
and then have fallen away, to renew them again to turning back, since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again for themselves and holding him up to public shame.

note.term: since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again

verse.note: Outside the New Testament this verb normally means simply “crucify,” but ancient Greek-speaking interpreters understood it here as “crucify again,” which suits the context and is followed by most translations. The clause can also be read as “while they are crucifying,” which would limit the impossibility to the time they persist in this stance. The scope of the warning in verses 4–6 is among the most debated questions in the letter.

verse.text: For ground that drinks the rain that often falls on it and bears a crop useful to those for whose sake it is farmed receives a share of blessing from God.
But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
But about you, dear friends, we are convinced of better things, things that go with salvation, even though we speak this way.
For God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you showed for his name when you served the holy ones, as you still do.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep; others use “God’s people.” The word refers to all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel, not to specially canonized or exceptionally virtuous individuals.

verse.text: We long for each of you to show the same eagerness for the full assurance of hope until the end,
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either complete certainty or complete fulfillment. On the second reading the author wants the readers’ eagerness to continue until their hope is fully realized. Most translations take it as assurance, as here.

verse.text: so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself,
saying, “I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply you.”

note.term: I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply you.

verse.note: The quotation is from Genesis 22:17, where, after Abraham’s offering of Isaac, God says “By myself I have sworn” (Genesis 22:16). The Greek reads literally “blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you,” reproducing a Hebrew idiom of emphasis, and opens with a particle that marks a solemn oath.

verse.text: And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham obtained the promise.
For people swear by someone greater than themselves, and for them the oath, given as confirmation, is the end of every dispute.
So God, wanting to show even more clearly to the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his purpose was, guaranteed it with an oath,
so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope set before us.
verse.note: The two things are generally understood to be God’s promise and the oath added to it. The author’s point is that either alone would be reliable, and the oath was added for the sake of the hearers’ confidence.

note.term: to take hold of the hope set before us

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in two ways: “we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope,” as here, or “we who have fled to take hold of the hope might have strong encouragement.” Translations are divided, and the overall sense differs little.

verse.text: We have this hope as an anchor of the soul, secure and firm, and it enters the inner place behind the curtain,

note.term: the inner place behind the curtain

verse.note: The curtain separated the innermost room of the tabernacle, the Most Holy Place, from the rest of the sanctuary; only the high priest passed behind it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The author uses it as an image of God’s own presence in heaven, which Jesus has entered.

verse.text: where Jesus has entered as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

note.term: according to the order of Melchizedek

verse.note: The phrase comes from Psalm 110:4, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” already quoted at 5:6. Melchizedek is the priest-king of Salem who meets Abraham in Genesis 14:18–20. The verse returns to the subject broken off at 5:10 and introduces the extended argument of chapter 7.

verse.text: For this Melchizedek—king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham as he was returning from the defeat of the kings and blessed him,
verse.note: Melchizedek appears in Genesis 14:17–20, where he meets Abraham after a battle, blesses him and receives a tenth of the spoils. Otherwise he appears only in Psalm 110:4, which is quoted in verses 17 and 21. The whole chapter is an argument built on these two passages.

verse.text: and to whom Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything; who is first, by the translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace;
without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God—remains a priest for all time.

note.term: without father, without mother, without genealogy

verse.note: Genesis records no parents, ancestry, birth or death for Melchizedek. Priestly office in Israel depended on documented descent, so the silence is striking, and the author reads it as a picture of a priesthood that neither rests on ancestry nor comes to an end. Most interpreters take this as an argument from what Scripture leaves unsaid; a minority think the author regarded Melchizedek as a heavenly being.

verse.text: Consider how great this man is, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest spoils—the patriarch himself!

Now those of the sons of Levi who receive the priestly office have a command, according to the Law, to collect a tenth from the people—that is, from their brothers—even though they have come from the loins of Abraham.
verse.note: The Greek uses the ordinary word for “a tenth” and verbs formed from it throughout this passage. “Tithe” means the same thing and is the usual rendering, but the plain number keeps the link between Abraham’s gift in verses 2 and 4 and the Levites’ entitlement. The command referred to is in Numbers 18:21–28.

verse.text: But the one whose genealogy is not traced from them has collected a tenth from Abraham and has blessed the one who has the promises.
And beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.
Here, people who die receive tenths; but there, it is one of whom it is testified that he lives.
And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tenths, has paid a tenth,
for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.

If, then, perfection had come through the Levitical priesthood—for on the basis of it the people received the Law—what further need would there have been for a different priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be named according to the order of Aaron?
verse.note: In Hebrews this word and the related verb in verses 19 and 28 speak of being brought to an intended goal, not of moral flawlessness. Here the goal is full and lasting access to God, as verse 19 indicates. Scholars differ on whether the word also carries an overtone of priestly consecration from its use in the Greek Old Testament.

note.term: on the basis of it the people received the Law
note.traditional: under it the people received the law

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean “on the basis of” or “concerning.” On the first reading the Law given to the people rests on the priesthood as its foundation; on the second the Law simply contains regulations about the priesthood. The first fits verse 12, where a change of priesthood entails a change of law, and is the more common view.

verse.text: For when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of law as well.
For the one about whom these things are said belongs to a different tribe, from which no one has served at the altar.
For it is plain that our Lord has sprung from Judah, a tribe about which Moses said nothing concerning priests.

note.traditional: sprang out of Judah; was descended from Judah

verse.note: The verb is used of the sun or a star rising and of a plant sprouting, not normally of family descent. In the Greek Old Testament it and its related noun are tied to messianic images: the star rising from Jacob (Numbers 24:17) and the “Branch” of David’s line (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 6:12). Many translations render it simply “descended,” which loses that echo.

verse.text: And this is even more abundantly clear if a different priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek,
one who has become a priest not according to the law of a commandment concerned with the flesh but according to the power of an indestructible life.

note.term: a commandment concerned with the flesh

verse.note: The adjective means “made of flesh” or “belonging to the flesh.” Most interpreters take it to refer to the rule that priests must be physical descendants of Aaron, and several translations paraphrase as “a requirement concerning bodily descent.” It may also suggest that such a rule belongs to the realm of what is mortal, in contrast to “an indestructible life.” It does not here mean sinful.

verse.text: For it is testified: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.”
For on the one hand a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness
(for the Law perfected nothing), and on the other hand a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
And this was not without an oath. The others have become priests without an oath,
but he with an oath, through the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever.’”

note.traditional: Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add “according to the order of Melchizedek” here. Several early witnesses lack the words, and they were probably added by copyists to match the fuller quotation of Psalm 110:4 in verse 17.

verse.text: To that same degree Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.
And the others who have become priests are many, because death prevents them from remaining;
but he, because he remains forever, holds his priesthood permanently.
verse.note: The word occurs only here in the New Testament. In period usage it means “permanent, inviolable,” and this is the sense standard lexicons give. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, take it as “not passing to a successor,” which fits the context well but is not clearly attested for the word.

verse.text: Therefore he is also able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can express degree (“completely, fully”) or time (“for all time, forever”). Both fit the context, since the argument rests on Jesus living always, and the author may intend both. The traditional “to the uttermost” leans toward degree, as does the rendering here.

verse.text: For such a high priest was indeed fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and raised higher than the heavens.
He has no need, as the high priests do, to offer up sacrifices day after day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered up himself.
verse.note: The sacrifice in which the high priest offered first for his own sins and then for the people’s belongs to the annual Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), not to the daily service. The author may be combining that rite with the daily offerings as one picture of ceaseless sacrifice, or may mean that the high priest’s need recurred continually. Interpreters are not agreed.

verse.text: For the Law appoints as high priests human beings who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the Law, appoints a Son who has been perfected forever.
Now the main point of what is being said is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens,
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either the chief point of an argument or a summary of it. Older versions took it as “the sum” of what has been said. Most modern scholars prefer “main point,” because what follows introduces new material and does not merely recapitulate.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; some keep the plural here.

verse.text: a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tent, which the Lord pitched, not a human being.
verse.note: The Greek is a plural form of “holy” used as a noun. Grammatically it could mean “the holy ones” (people) or “the holy things,” but in Hebrews this neuter plural regularly names the holy place of the tent-sanctuary, and its pairing with “the true tent” confirms that sense here. “The sanctuary” is therefore used here, not “holy ones,” as in most modern versions; some render it “the holy places.”

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel’s portable wilderness sanctuary. “Tabernacle,” found in older versions and some modern ones, now sounds like a special religious object and hides the plain image. Several modern versions also use “tent” in Hebrews.

verse.text: For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices; so it is necessary for this one too to have something to offer.
Now if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer the gifts according to the law.

These serve a sketch and shadow of the heavenly things, just as Moses was instructed by God when he was about to construct the tent; for he says, “See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.”
verse.note: Many versions have “copy” here, and the KJV has “example.” In the usage of the period the word denotes an example, model, or outline, not a replica, so “sketch” is used, as in some modern versions. The point is that the earthly sanctuary gives only an outline of the heavenly reality.

note.term: See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.

verse.note: The quotation is from Exodus 25:40, where God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai about building the wilderness sanctuary. The author takes the “pattern” shown to Moses as implying a heavenly original of which the earthly tent is only a likeness.

verse.text: But as it is, he has obtained a ministry as much more excellent as the covenant he mediates is better, a covenant enacted on better promises.
For if that first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second.
For finding fault with them he says: “Look, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will conclude a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,
verse.note: Manuscripts differ over the case of the pronoun “them.” With the reading adopted here, God finds fault with the people; with the other, the words could also be read “finding fault, he says to them,” leaving the fault to lie with the first covenant itself. Either way the phrase picks up “faultless” in the previous verse.
Verses 8–12 quote Jeremiah 31:31–34 in its Greek form (chapter 38 in the Septuagint). It is the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and the author returns to it in chapter 10.

text.q: not like the covenant that I made with their ancestors on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

verse.note: The author quotes the Greek version of Jeremiah, which differs here from the traditional Hebrew text. The Hebrew is usually translated “though I was their husband,” so English Old Testaments read differently at Jeremiah 31:32.

text.q: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.
And they will never teach, each one his fellow citizen and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
For I will be merciful toward their wrongdoings, and I will never again remember their sins.”

verse.text: In saying “new,” he has made the first one obsolete; and what is becoming obsolete and growing old is close to vanishing.
verse.note: The verb means “to make old” or “to treat as old,” answering the word “new” in the quotation, and the same verb is repeated in “becoming obsolete.” It can be taken as declaring the first covenant old or as actually rendering it so. “Obsolete” is the common modern rendering; the KJV has “made the first old.”

verse.text: Now the first covenant had its requirements for worship and its sanctuary, an earthly one.
verse.note: Elsewhere this translation renders the word “righteous requirement,” but here and in verse 10 it means a prescribed rule for the conduct of worship, with no stress on rightness. “Righteous requirements for the flesh” in verse 10 would mislead, so the adjective is dropped while “requirements” keeps the link to the word’s other uses. Most translations have “regulations” or “ordinances.”

verse.text: For a tent was set up, the first one, in which were the lampstand and the table and the setting out of the loaves; this is called the Holy Place.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel’s portable wilderness sanctuary. “Tabernacle,” the older English rendering, now sounds like a special religious object and hides the plain image; several modern translations also use “tent” in Hebrews. In this passage the author calls each of the sanctuary’s two rooms a “tent.”

note.term: the setting out of the loaves
note.traditional: the showbread; the bread of the Presence

verse.note: The Greek says literally “the setting out of the loaves,” the Greek Old Testament’s expression for the twelve loaves laid out before God each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9). “Showbread” and “bread of the Presence” are the traditional English names, the latter reflecting the Hebrew rather than the Greek.

verse.text: Behind the second curtain was a tent called the Holy of Holies,

which had a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold. In the ark were a golden jar holding the manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant,

note.traditional: golden censer; golden altar of incense

verse.note: The word can mean either a censer or an incense altar; most modern translations choose the altar. In Exodus the incense altar stood in front of the curtain, not behind it. The author may link it with the inner room because of its role in the Day of Atonement rite, but the point is debated.

verse.text: and above it were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the place of atonement. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word names the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The traditional “mercy seat” suggests a chair; “place of atonement” says what the object was for. The same phrase is used for this word in Romans 3:25, where its exact sense is disputed.

verse.text: With these things set up in this way, the priests go continually into the first tent, carrying out their acts of worship,
but into the second only the high priest goes, once a year, and not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the sins the people have committed in ignorance.
verse.note: This refers to the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), when the high priest entered the inner room with the blood of a bull for himself and of a goat for the people. That yearly rite is the pattern behind the argument of the whole chapter.

verse.text: By this the Holy Spirit makes clear that the way into the sanctuary has not yet been revealed while the first tent is still standing.

note.traditional: the holiest of all; the holy places; the sanctuary

verse.note: The Greek is a plural, literally “the holy places” or “the holy things.” The same word is the name of the outer room in verse 2, but here and in verses 12, 24 and 25 it denotes the inner place of God’s presence, so “sanctuary” is used. “The first tent” in this verse may mean the outer room, as in verses 2 and 6, or the whole earthly tent as the sanctuary of the first covenant; the wording leaves both open.

verse.text: That tent is a symbol for the present time, and in keeping with it gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshiper perfect in conscience.
They deal only with foods and drinks and various washings—requirements for the flesh, imposed until the time when things are set right.
But when Christ arrived as high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent—not made by hands, that is, not of this creation—

note.term: the good things that have come

verse.note: Some early manuscripts read “the good things that have come”; many others read “the good things to come.” The SBLGNT and most recent editions and translations follow the former, while the KJV and some others follow the latter.

verse.text: and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, he entered the sanctuary once for all and secured eternal redemption.
For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who have been defiled, make them holy so that their flesh is clean,
verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “make holy” keeps that link visible. “Sanctify,” used by most traditional versions, means the same but now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement, which is not the point here. The reference is to ritual cleansing, including the ashes of the red heifer in Numbers 19.

verse.text: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works so that we may serve the living God!
verse.note: The Greek has no article (“through eternal spirit”). Most interpreters and translations take this as the Holy Spirit. Others understand Christ’s own eternal spirit or nature, in contrast to the perishable animals of the old sacrifices.

verse.text: And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who have been called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has taken place for redemption from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
For where there is a will, the death of the one who made it has to be established;
verse.note: The same Greek word is translated “covenant” in verses 15 and 18–20 and “will” here and in verse 17. In everyday Greek it meant a last will and testament, while the Greek Old Testament used it for God’s covenant. Most translators hold that the author plays on both senses, helped by “inheritance” in verse 15. A minority keep “covenant” throughout, taking the death to be that of the sacrificial animals that stood for the covenant-maker when a covenant was ratified.

verse.text: for a will becomes valid only at death, since it is never in force while the one who made it is alive.
That is why not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

For when Moses had spoken every commandment in accordance with the Law to all the people, he took the blood of the calves, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the scroll itself and all the people,

note.traditional: the blood of calves and goats

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “the blood of the calves and the goats,” and most English translations follow them. The SBLGNT prints the shorter reading, on the view that the longer one is an expansion influenced by verse 12. The question remains open.

verse.text: saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.”
And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels of the ministry.
Indeed, according to the Law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
So it was necessary for the copies of the things in the heavens to be cleansed by these means, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.
For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by hands, a counterpart of the true one, but heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God on our behalf.
Nor did he enter to offer himself many times, as the high priest enters the sanctuary year after year with blood that is not his own,
for then he would have had to suffer many times since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has been revealed once, at the end of the ages, to do away with sin by his sacrifice.
And just as it is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment,
so also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will be seen a second time, apart from sin, by those who eagerly await him, for salvation.

note.traditional: without sin; not to deal with sin

verse.note: The phrase is literally “without sin.” It does not contrast a sinless second coming with a sinful first. It means that the second appearing has nothing to do with dealing with sin, which was done once. Many translations paraphrase as “not to deal with sin.” The closing “for salvation” may go with “will be seen” or with “await him.”

verse.text: For since the Law has a shadow of the good things to come and not the very form of the realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are offered continually year after year, make perfect those who draw near.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to bring someone to the intended goal or completed state, not to make morally flawless. In Hebrews it describes worshipers being fully fitted to come into God’s presence, something the yearly sacrifices could not achieve. The traditional “make perfect” is kept, in its older sense of “complete.”

verse.text: Otherwise, would they not have stopped being offered, since the worshipers, cleansed once for all, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins year after year,
for it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
Therefore, when Christ comes into the world, he says: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you prepared for me;

note.term: a body you prepared for me

verse.note: Verses 5–7 quote Psalm 40:6–8 in its ancient Greek version, which the author hears as the words of Christ; the Greek leaves the speaker unnamed, and “Christ” is supplied from the preceding sentence. Where the Hebrew text has “ears you have dug for me,” the Greek version cited here reads “a body you prepared for me,” and the argument in verse 10 depends on that wording.

text.q: in whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure.
Then I said, ‘Look, I have come—in the scroll of the book it is written about me—to do your will, O God.’”

verse.text: After saying above, “Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and sin offerings you did not desire, nor did you take pleasure in them,” though these are offered according to the Law,
he then says, “Look, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.
And by that will we have been made holy through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verse.note: The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” and means to bring someone into the sphere of what belongs to God. Most translations use “sanctified,” which hides that link and now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement. The meaning is not disputed; the choice is one of clarity.

verse.text: And every priest stands day after day performing his service and offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never remove sins.
But this one, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of God,
verse.note: The phrase can go with what precedes (“one sacrifice for sins for all time”) or with what follows (“sat down for all time at the right hand of God”). Either fits the contrast with priests who stand and offer repeatedly, and translations and commentators are divided. The rendering here leaves it with the sacrifice.

verse.text: waiting from then on until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet.
For by one offering he has made perfect for all time those who are being made holy.
And the Holy Spirit also testifies to us, for after saying,

text.q: “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and on their minds I will write them,”

verse.text: he adds, “and their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more.”
verse.note: The Greek has no words corresponding to “he adds”; the sentence begun with “after saying” in verse 15 is left without an explicit continuation. Most translations supply one here, so that the promise to remember sins no more is the point being drawn out. Some instead take the continuation to begin at “says the Lord” in verse 16.

verse.text: Now where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
Therefore, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the sanctuary by the blood of Jesus,
verse.note: The Greek plural, literally “brothers,” was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as members of one family. “Brothers and sisters” gives a modern reader that sense. Many recent translations do the same, while others keep “brothers.”

The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind, and by this period also the assurance of someone who can come before a superior without fear or shame. “Confidence” conveys that better than the traditional “boldness,” which can suggest audacity. Many modern versions also have “confidence” here; the difference is one of English nuance, not of meaning.

verse.text: by the new and living way that he inaugurated for us through the curtain, that is, his flesh,

note.traditional: that is to say, his flesh

verse.note: The phrase most naturally explains “the curtain”: Christ’s flesh, given up in death, is what the way into the sanctuary passes through. Some interpreters attach it to “way” instead, meaning the way opened by his human life and death, to avoid picturing his flesh as a barrier. The Greek allows both, and the wording here follows the majority reading.

verse.text: and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
And let us give thought to one another, to stir up love and good works,
not abandoning our gathering together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.
verse.note: “The day” is shorthand for the day of the Lord, the time of God’s judgment and deliverance announced by the prophets, which the first Christians connected with Christ’s return. The original readers needed no further explanation.

verse.text: For if we deliberately go on sinning after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains any sacrifice for sins,
but a terrifying expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire about to consume the adversaries.
Anyone who has rejected the Law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

How much worse a punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, regarded as common the blood of the covenant by which he was made holy, and insulted the Spirit of grace?
verse.note: The Greek word means “ordinary,” the opposite of what is set apart for God, and in Jewish usage it could carry the sense “ritually unclean.” To regard the covenant blood as common is to treat it as no different from any other blood. “Common” keeps the contrast with “made holy”; most translations have “unholy” or “profaned.”

verse.text: For we know the one who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge his people.”
It is a terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
But remember the earlier days, when, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle with sufferings,
at times being made a public spectacle by insults and afflictions, and at times becoming partners with those who were treated that way.
For you suffered along with the prisoners, and you accepted the seizure of your possessions with joy, knowing that you yourselves have a better possession, and a lasting one.
verse.note: Some later manuscripts read “my chains” instead of “the prisoners,” making the sentence refer to the author’s own imprisonment, and add “in heaven” after “possession.” The King James Version follows both readings. The shorter text translated here is generally judged to be the earlier one.

verse.text: So do not throw away your confidence, which carries a great reward.
For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive what was promised.
For “in just a very little while, the one who is coming will come and will not delay;

note.term: the one who is coming will come

verse.note: Verses 37–38 quote Habakkuk 2:3–4 in its ancient Greek version, introduced by a phrase from Isaiah 26:20 (“a very little while”). The author reverses the order of the two clauses of Habakkuk 2:4, so that “shrinks back” is said of the righteous one, and understands “the one who is coming” as the returning Christ.

text.q: but my righteous one will live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul takes no pleasure in him.”

verse.note: The Greek word covers both “faith” and “faithfulness,” and Habakkuk’s Hebrew speaks of the righteous person’s steadfastness; some manuscripts of the Greek version have “by my faithfulness,” meaning God’s. Hebrews places “my” with “righteous one,” though a few manuscripts differ, and goes on in the next chapter to describe faith as trust that holds firm. “Faith” is therefore used, with steadfast loyalty as part of what is meant.

verse.text: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
Now faith is the reality of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.

note.term: the reality of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen
note.traditional: the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen (KJV); the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen (most modern versions)

verse.note: Most modern versions make faith an inner state: “assurance” and “conviction.” In the usage of the period the first noun normally names something objective, what underlies a thing or gives it substance, and the second means proof or demonstration, not the feeling of being convinced. Many commentators favor this objective sense, but scholarship is divided and “assurance” is still widely defended.

verse.text: For by it the ancients had witness borne to them.

note.traditional: obtained a good report (KJV); were commended; received approval

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary one for giving testimony, used here and in verses 4, 5 and 39 for the favorable witness that God or Scripture bears to these figures. Modern versions usually paraphrase as “were commended” or “received approval,” which states the sense fairly. The witness language is kept because the author builds on it, arriving at the “cloud of witnesses” in 12:1.

verse.text: By faith we understand that the universe was set in order by God’s word, so that what is seen did not come into being from things that are visible.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “the ages,” a time-word that here and in 1:2 stands for the whole created order, as standard lexicons recognize. Older versions have “the worlds”; several modern versions also have “the universe.”

verse.text: By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain, and through it witness was borne that he was righteous, God himself bearing witness over his gifts; and through it, though he died, he still speaks.
By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him away. For before he was taken away, witness is borne that he had pleased God,
and without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

By faith Noah, warned by God about things not yet seen, in reverent fear built an ark to save his household. Through this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that accords with faith.
By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed and set out for a place he was going to receive as an inheritance, and he set out not knowing where he was going.
By faith he lived as a resident foreigner in the land of the promise, as in a land not his own, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise.
For he was waiting for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
By faith, together with Sarah herself, he received power to father offspring, even past the normal age, since he considered faithful the one who had promised.

note.term: together with Sarah herself, he received power to father offspring
note.traditional: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive

verse.note: The traditional rendering makes Sarah the subject. But the Greek phrase rendered “to father offspring” is the regular idiom for the male role in conception, and Abraham is the subject of the verses on either side. The edition translated here prints “Sarah herself” in a form meaning “together with Sarah”; in the earliest manuscripts that form and the subject form were written identically, and some manuscripts add “barren.” Both readings have strong scholarly support.

verse.text: Therefore from one man, and one as good as dead at that, there were born descendants like the stars of the sky in number and like the countless sand along the seashore.
All these died in faith, without receiving the promises, but they saw them from afar and greeted them, and they confessed that they were strangers and temporary residents on the earth.
For people who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.
If they had been thinking of the one they had left, they would have had opportunity to return.
But as it is, they long for a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. He who had received the promises was offering up his one and only son,
verse.note: The word means the only one of its kind; its second half comes from the word for “kind,” not “beget,” though a minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.” Abraham also had Ishmael, so Isaac is “one and only” as the unique son through whom the promise was to run.

verse.text: he to whom it had been said, “Through Isaac your offspring will be named.”
He reasoned that God was able to raise people even from the dead, and from the dead, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “in a parable.” It may mean simply “in a manner of speaking,” since Isaac did not actually die. It may also mean “as a symbol,” so that Isaac’s return prefigures resurrection, perhaps that of Christ. The rendering leaves both open.

verse.text: By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even concerning things to come.
By faith Jacob, as he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and bowed in worship over the top of his staff.

note.term: bowed in worship over the top of his staff
note.traditional: worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff

verse.note: The author quotes Genesis 47:31 in its Greek form. The Hebrew consonants there can be read as either “staff” or “bed”; the Greek translators read “staff,” while the traditional Hebrew vocalization gives “bed.” The verb names a physical bowing in reverence, here directed to God.

verse.text: By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, spoke of the exodus of the sons of Israel and gave instructions about his bones.
By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.
By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called a son of Pharaoh’s daughter,
choosing to be mistreated along with the people of God rather than to have the short-lived enjoyment of sin,
considering the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.
verse.note: The phrase may mean abuse suffered for the sake of the coming Christ, or abuse of the same kind that Christ himself bore (compare 13:13). It may also echo Psalm 89:50–51, where God’s “anointed” is reproached, so that Moses shares the disgrace of God’s anointed people. The author does not explain how Moses knew of Christ, and interpreters differ.

verse.text: By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he held firm as one who sees him who is unseen.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them.
By faith they crossed the Red Sea as if over dry land, but when the Egyptians tried it, they were swallowed up.
By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been circled for seven days.
By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who had disobeyed, because she had welcomed the spies in peace.
And what more shall I say? For time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets,
who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions,
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). Since the list concerns judges, kings and prophets, the phrase most likely means that they ruled or judged justly, as many modern versions take it. It could also mean more generally that they did what was right.

verse.text: quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, routed foreign armies.
Women received their dead back by resurrection. Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection.

note.term: Others were tortured, refusing to accept release

verse.note: The women who received their dead back are the widow of Zarephath and the woman of Shunem (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4). The verb for “tortured” refers to being stretched on a frame and beaten. Most interpreters see an allusion to the martyrs of the Maccabean period, who according to 2 Maccabees 6–7 refused to save their lives by renouncing the Law and died in hope of resurrection.

verse.text: Still others experienced mocking and flogging, and even chains and prison.
They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, mistreated.

note.traditional: they were sawn asunder, were tempted

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “they were tested” (KJV “were tempted”) before or after this phrase. The edition translated here omits it, judging it a copying error. Jewish tradition held that the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two.

verse.text: The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, in caves and in holes in the ground.
And all these, though witness was borne to them through their faith, did not receive what was promised,
since God had provided something better for us, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us.
Therefore, since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us, let us also lay aside every weight and the sin that so easily entangles, and run with endurance the race set before us,

note.term: the sin that so easily entangles
note.traditional: the sin which doth so easily beset us

verse.note: The Greek adjective occurs nowhere else in surviving literature before this verse, so its exact sense is uncertain. Most scholars take it as “easily surrounding” or “clinging closely,” which suits the picture of a runner stripping off anything that hampers; “easily distracting” is the reading of one very early manuscript. The rendering here follows the majority view.

verse.text: fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured a cross, scorning the shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.

note.traditional: the author and finisher of our faith

verse.note: The first word means a leader who goes first and opens the way for others, and can also mean a founder or originator; “pioneer” (as in several modern versions) fits the race imagery better than “author.” The Greek has no “our”: Jesus is presented as the one who both leads the way in faith and brings it to its goal, not only as the source of the readers’ own faith. “Perfecter” belongs to the same word-family as “made perfect” in verse 23.

note.term: for the joy set before him
note.traditional: for the joy that was set before him

verse.note: The preposition can mean “for the sake of” or “instead of.” Most interpreters take it as the former: Jesus endured the cross to gain the joy that lay ahead. A minority read “instead of the joy that lay within his reach, he endured a cross.” The same preposition is used in verse 16 of Esau selling his birthright “for” a meal.

verse.text: For consider him who has endured such opposition from sinners against themselves, so that you may not grow weary in your souls and lose heart.
verse.note: The Greek text translated here reads the plural “against themselves,” which has strong support in the earliest manuscripts; other manuscripts, followed by most English versions, read the singular “against himself.” With the plural, the thought is that the sinners’ opposition to Jesus was to their own harm, perhaps echoing the description of Korah’s company in Numbers 16:38. Many scholars regard the plural as the harder reading and are divided over which is original.

verse.text: You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin,
and you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, nor lose heart when you are corrected by him;
verse.note: The Greek word covers the whole upbringing of a child: instruction, training and correction, including punishment. “Discipline” is used throughout the passage in that broad sense, not as a synonym for punishment alone. The quotation is Proverbs 3:11–12 in its Greek form, whose second line (“flogs every son he accepts”) differs from the Hebrew, “as a father the son in whom he delights.”

text.q: for the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and flogs every son he accepts.”
