verse.text: It is for discipline that you endure. God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?
But if you are without the discipline in which all have come to share, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
Besides, we had our fathers in the flesh to discipline us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?
For they disciplined us for a few days as seemed best to them, but he does it for our benefit, so that we may share in his holiness.
No discipline seems at the time to be a matter of joy, but of grief; later, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
Therefore set straight the drooping hands and the weakened knees,
and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “turn aside,” and some take it so here: the lame should not be made to stray from the path. It was also used by medical writers for a limb being dislocated, and the contrast with “be healed” favors that sense, which most modern versions adopt.

verse.text: Pursue peace with everyone, and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord,
watching that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness grows up and causes trouble, and through it many are defiled,
that no one is sexually immoral or profane like Esau, who for a single meal sold his own birthright.
For you know that afterward, when he did want to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for turning back, though he sought it with tears.
verse.note: The traditional “repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word denotes a change of direction, a reversal. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term. Some scholars think the phrase here is close to a legal idiom, “no opportunity for reversal,” meaning that Esau could not get the decision changed.

note.term: though he sought it with tears
note.traditional: though he sought it carefully with tears

verse.note: “It” could refer either to the blessing or to the turning back; both nouns are feminine in Greek. In Genesis 27:34–38 Esau weeps and pleads for the blessing, which favors the first, but the nearer noun is “turning back,” and interpreters are divided. The English leaves the reference as open as the Greek.

verse.text: For you have not come to something that can be touched and a blazing fire, to darkness and gloom and storm,

note.traditional: the mount that might be touched

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no word for “mountain” here; later manuscripts add it, probably to match “Mount Zion” in verse 22. The scene is Mount Sinai at the giving of the Law (Exodus 19–20; Deuteronomy 4–5), which the first readers would have recognized from the fire, darkness, trumpet and voice without its being named.

verse.text: and a trumpet blast and a voice speaking words—a voice whose hearers refused to have any further word spoken to them,
verse.note: Most versions have “begged that no further word be spoken.” The verb means to ask to be excused from something, to decline or refuse, and it is the same verb used twice in verse 25 (“do not refuse the one who is speaking”). It is rendered “refuse” in both places so that the link the author draws between Israel at Sinai and the readers is visible.

verse.text: for they could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”
Indeed, so fearful was the sight that Moses said, “I am full of fear and trembling.”
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering,

note.traditional: to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn

verse.note: The word means a festival gathering. It can be attached to what precedes (“myriads of angels in festal gathering”), as here and in most modern versions, or to what follows (“to a festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn”), which is how some editions punctuate the Greek. The sense of the whole is little affected.

verse.text: and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and was the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God; “church” now suggests a building or an institution. Nearly all translations use “church,” and readers generally know what it refers to. “Assembly” is used here to keep the first-century sense, which suits this picture of a people gathered at the mountain.

verse.text: and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel.

note.traditional: that speaketh better things than that of Abel

verse.note: In Genesis 4:10 Abel’s blood cries out to God from the ground, a cry usually understood as a call for justice; Hebrews 11:4 says that Abel, though dead, still speaks. The blood of Jesus, pictured as sprinkled like the blood that sealed the covenant at Sinai, speaks a better message. The Greek says simply “than Abel”; many versions expand to “than the blood of Abel.”

verse.text: See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused the one who warned them on earth, much less will we, if we turn away from the one who warns from the heavens.
His voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heaven.”
Now this “Yet once more” points to the removal of the things that are shaken, as things that have been made, so that the things that are not shaken may remain.
Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be grateful, and so serve God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe,
verse.note: The Greek phrase “have grace” was a common idiom for “be thankful,” and most modern versions take it that way. The older rendering, “let us have grace” (that is, hold on to God’s grace), is also possible, since the same noun means “grace” in verse 15.

verse.text: for our God is indeed a consuming fire.
Let brotherly love endure.
Do not forget to show hospitality, for through it some have hosted angels without knowing it.
Remember the prisoners as though imprisoned with them, and those who are mistreated, since you yourselves are also in a body.
Let marriage be held in honor by all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

note.term: Let marriage be held in honor by all

verse.note: The Greek has no verb here. Most translations supply a command, which fits the surrounding instructions, but a statement (“Marriage is honorable”) is also grammatically possible. The phrase rendered “by all” could instead mean “in every respect.”

verse.text: Let your way of life be free from the love of money, and be content with what you have, for he himself has said, “I will never leave you, and I will never abandon you.”
So we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can a human being do to me?”
Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Look closely at the outcome of their conduct, and imitate their faith.
verse.note: The past tense “spoke” and the word “outcome” suggest that these are the community's earlier leaders, who have since died. The “outcome” is most likely how their lives ended, faithful to the last. Whether martyrdom is implied is not stated.

verse.text: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.
Do not be carried away by varied and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be made firm by grace, not by foods, which have been of no benefit to those who live by them.
verse.note: The author is opposing a teaching that treated certain foods or sacred meals as spiritually strengthening. The following verses, about an altar and eating from sacrifices, suggest a connection with Jewish food rules or sacrificial meals. The exact practice in view is debated.

verse.text: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for a tent, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel's portable wilderness sanctuary. “Tabernacle” is the traditional rendering and is kept by some modern versions, while others also use “tent” in Hebrews. The plain word lets the reader hear what a first-century reader heard.

verse.text: For the bodies of the animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin are burned outside the camp.
verse.note: On the Day of Atonement the blood of the sin offerings was carried into the inner sanctuary, and the carcasses were not eaten by the priests but burned outside Israel's camp (Leviticus 16). The author sees the same pattern in Jesus' death outside the city gate. Most interpreters take the “altar” of verse 10 as a figure for his sacrifice, though some see a reference to the Lord's Supper.

verse.text: That is why Jesus also suffered outside the gate, to make the people holy through his own blood.
verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy” and means to bring someone into the sphere of what belongs to God. Most traditional versions use “sanctify,” which hides that link and now suggests to many readers a doctrine of gradual moral improvement. Several modern translations also use “make holy,” and the meaning itself is not in dispute.

verse.text: So then, let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore.
For here we have no enduring city, but we are seeking the one that is to come.
Through him, then, let us continually offer up to God a sacrifice of praise—that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
verse.note: The verb can mean to acknowledge or profess openly, and in language shaped by the Greek Old Testament it can also mean to give thanks or praise. Older versions have “giving thanks to his name,” and either sense fits a “sacrifice of praise.” “The fruit of lips” echoes the Greek version of Hosea 14.

verse.text: And do not forget to do good and to share, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.

Obey your leaders and yield to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning—for that would be of no advantage to you.
verse.note: In this form the verb ranges from “be persuaded by” and “trust” to “heed” and “obey.” With a person as its object, “obey” or “follow” is the usual sense, and most translations render it so. Some prefer “have confidence in.” The same verb is translated “we are convinced” in verse 18.

verse.text: Pray for us, for we are convinced that we have a good conscience, wanting to conduct ourselves well in every way.
I urge you all the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you sooner.
Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of an eternal covenant,
equip you with every good thing to do his will, working in us what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever. Amen.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “in you” instead of “in us.” Manuscripts also vary elsewhere in this verse: some read “every good work” for “every good thing,” and many end with “forever and ever.” The translation follows the SBLGNT text.

verse.text: I urge you, brothers and sisters, bear with this word of exhortation, for in fact I have written to you briefly.
verse.note: The same phrase is used in Acts 13:15 for an address given in a synagogue after the Scripture readings, which suggests that Hebrews is a sermon put into writing. The noun is related to the verb translated “I urge” at the start of the verse. The claim to have written “briefly” is a conventional courtesy.

verse.text: Know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he comes soon, I will see you together with him.
Greet all your leaders and all the holy ones. Those from Italy send you greetings.
verse.note: The word refers to all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. “Saints,” the traditional rendering, now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints,” and others use “God's people.”

The Greek can mean people in Italy sending greetings abroad, or Italians living elsewhere sending greetings home. The second reading is one reason many scholars think the letter was sent to Rome. The question remains open.

verse.text: Grace be with you all.
